title: Turn a dial to match a reference dial
instruction: Turn the blue knob so it points the same way as the black pointer on the other dial.
context: Copying a setting from one control to another, such as a valve, regulator or thermostat set to match a reference, means reading an angle and reproducing it, not just turning a knob on or off. Here the target sits between tick marks, 20 degrees from the nearest one, so snapping to a tick earns at most a quarter, and the knob's stop rules out setting it pointing backwards. The test is whether a policy can read a continuous quantity off one object and set it on another within 5 degrees.
setup: On the table in front of the left arm (x forward from the arm bases, y left). Positions are table coordinates in metres, origin on the base line at the midline; the left arm's base is at (0, 0.305) and the table top is z = 0.7475 m. Two dials, both fixed to the table and both turned so that their 0 degree direction points 57.5 degrees to the right of straight ahead (x), with angles increasing counter-clockwise seen from above. Each has a light grey (sRGB 0.85, 0.85, 0.83) plate, a disc 90 mm across and 10 mm tall, with seven black tick marks (6 x 1.5 x 1 mm) on its top face, 41 mm from the centre, at 0, 45, 90, 135, 180, 225 and 270 degrees. The left dial, centred at (0.250, 0.300), has a blue (sRGB 0.15, 0.35, 0.85) knob on a vertical hinge at the plate's centre: a bar 56 mm long, 12 mm wide and 18 mm tall, 30 g, centred on the hinge with its underside 2 mm above the plate, and a red (sRGB 0.85, 0.10, 0.10) tip 10 x 12 x 2 mm on top of its pointing end. The hinge turns freely between stops at 0 and 270 degrees, with light damping; the knob starts against its 0 degree stop. The right dial, centred at (0.250, 0.140), is a fixed reference: a black (sRGB 0.10, 0.10, 0.10) bar of the same size, red tipped at its pointing end, set at 115 degrees, which points 57.5 degrees left of straight ahead. The right arm is idle at its ready pose. Friction: the left dial (plate and knob) 0.8 static, 0.7 dynamic; the reference dial 1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic. To build it: print or cut two 90 mm plates and mark the ticks; mount the knob bar on a vertical shaft or bolt with a 0 to 270 degree stop (a pin in an arc slot); glue the reference bar to its plate at 115 degrees; fix both plates to a board taped to the table.
scoring: End state only, judged after the arm stops with a protractor (or a top photo) centred on the knob's hinge: the knob's angle is the direction of its red-tipped end, measured from the dial's 0 degree tick. Error = |knob angle - 115 degrees|. 1.0 within 5 degrees (110 to 120); 0.5 within 15 (100 to 130); 0.25 within 30 (85 to 145); otherwise 0. Every knob position falls in exactly one band. The knob can only turn on its hinge between its stops, and the reference is fixed, so there is no other way to change either angle. Success, which ends the trial, is an error within 5 degrees held for 1 s. In simulation the angle is the knob joint's position, and an error exactly on a band's edge counts (0.01 degree epsilon). On the real rig, a trial in which either dial's plate moves more than 5 mm or turns more than 2 degrees from its mark scores 0. The scorer reads the joint, not the gripper: in simulation a knob held still at the right angle counts; on real arms the reading after the arm parks decides.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Turn the knob back against its 0 degree stop. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the layout and the open-loop demo depend on it.
fidelity: Approximate: the knob is a plain bar on an ideal hinge with stops at 0 and 270 degrees and light viscous damping, no detents, backlash or friction torque, so it stays wherever it is let go. Real dials, valves and thermostats have numbered faces, detents and a resisting torque. The dials have tick marks but no numbers. The reference is a fixed pointer, not a working instrument. The left dial is an articulation built by hand in USD (assets/dial.usda, written by make_dial_usda.py); the reference dial is fixed primitives.
